questions.prompt: Where are YOU with the puck?
questions.explanation: The puck is behind the left goal line, so YOU can use the net to change Gold 1’s angle; if Gold 1 follows, outlet picture changes.

questions.prompt: Which two facts make behind-net space useful?

options.text: Gold 1’s position on the centre-ice side of the goal line
D2’s possible support across the middle
The puck is already at centre ice

questions.explanation: The net, pressure and support change the possible routes. The picture does not guarantee an exit.

questions.prompt: Arrange one behind-net escape.

options.text: Carry behind net with puck protected
Recheck D2 and W before exiting

questions.explanation: Pressure side sets route; the net can screen the carry; final scan selects exit.

questions.prompt: Move D2 nearer the middle to compare an outlet from behind the net.
questions.explanation: The example is slightly farther from YOU than D2’s starting spot. Check the net and pressure before treating the changed angle as a usable pass.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 follows behind the net, what deserves a fresh read?

options.text: Whether W or D2 has a usable outlet angle

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s route changes pressure side, so compare W and D2; if both covered, protect and wait.

questions.prompt: How does the net change the forechecker’s approach without guaranteeing an exit?
questions.explanation: The net can change the available approach routes. Check the forechecker, receiver and passing lane rather than assuming the obstacle guarantees an exit.

questions.prompt: What has F1 done before this freeze?

questions.prompt: Which two things help YOU stay useful during the delay?

options.text: Remain at a different height from F1
Keep a route back toward puck
Rush past F1 into same lane

questions.explanation: Different height and connected route give F1 another option; rushing past removes delay’s purpose.

questions.prompt: Order one delayed-entry support.

options.text: Arrive when F1 can see connection

questions.explanation: Gold 1 sets open side; separation preserves lane; arriving visibly turns delay into support.

questions.prompt: Move YOU nearer the middle while staying behind F1 toward the blue line.
questions.explanation: The example changes the angle to F1 while keeping separation from D2. Recheck Gold 1 before offering the pass.

questions.prompt: If F1 loses control during the delay, what must YOU reassess first?

options.text: Where the new puck threat is and whether support becomes recovery
Calling for a pass from a player without puck

questions.explanation: Loss of control requires locating the puck and pressure again. A bobble alone does not establish Gold possession or a fixed recovery job.

questions.prompt: What does saving ice mean in this particular scene?
questions.explanation: Stay separated enough to offer support while checking F1, D2 and pressure. Whether to keep that space or move depends on the next cue.

questions.prompt: What is crowded in this freeze?

questions.prompt: Which two reset cues are visible?

options.text: Both Navy players are below goal line

questions.explanation: High separation and weak-side support give W outlets away from slot; low crowding would leave no reset.

questions.prompt: Arrange one crowded-slot reset.

options.text: Recheck an attacking route before using it

questions.explanation: Compare the slot traffic with high support and reassess the available routes. A reset does not force the defenders to move.

questions.prompt: Move YOU nearer the blue line to compare a reset angle from W.
questions.explanation: The example remains outside the low cluster and changes the route from W. Check both defenders and D2 before using it.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 follows YOU high, what might help W?

options.text: Check whether D2’s weak-side lane is now usable

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s movement can uncover D2, so use changed coverage; if D2 covered, protect and wait.

questions.prompt: Why is a reset a positive action here?
questions.explanation: It moves possession from two slot defenders and preserves an attack after coverage shifts; if high lane is covered too, keeping puck beats forcing.

questions.prompt: What is the puck state?

options.text: Loose in a wide lane deep in Navy’s zone

questions.explanation: The puck marker is loose, so YOU read a retrieval race while D1 protects inside; if control changes, roles update.

questions.prompt: Which two jobs need separating?

options.text: A retrieval attempt if YOU can reach the puck

questions.explanation: Coordinate the puck contest and inside coverage. Proximity alone does not assign a guaranteed retrieval.

questions.prompt: Arrange one failed-clear recovery.

options.text: YOU retrieve if lane is reachable

questions.explanation: Call the loose puck and coordinate reachable roles. D1’s position can help cover Gold 1 but does not guarantee a stopped attack.

questions.prompt: Move D1 to compare a position nearer Navy’s net than Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The example keeps D1 net-side of Gold 1 while YOU approach the loose puck. Reassess both threats if possession changes.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 gains clear control, what changes?

options.text: Reassess the new carrier and agree coverage with D1
Both defenders remain tied to wall

questions.explanation: Clear control changes puck threat, so D1’s coverage and your recovery update; if Navy recovers, rebuild support.

questions.prompt: Why is a failed clear a role-change moment?
questions.explanation: The blocked puck removes assumption of exit, so one retrieves and another protects slot; if possession becomes clear, both jobs change.
